exec_orders_scope.t: When Congress won't act, a president should wait, acting alone only on how the executive branch runs.
yes: Executive orders limited to managing federal agencies
no: Presidents making new policy without Congress

exec_orders_scope.t: A president should act alone only in emergencies.
yes: Unilateral action in true emergencies
no: Executive orders to get around Congress in normal times

exec_orders_scope.t: A president can act alone where existing laws leave room to decide.
yes: Executive orders that use discretion existing laws give

exec_orders_scope.t: A president can act alone through executive orders whenever it seems necessary.
yes: Broad use of executive orders when Congress won't act, by any president

refuse_to_spend.t: A president must spend money as Congress directed.
yes: No delays or refusals to spend approved funds

refuse_to_spend.t: A president can briefly delay spending while asking Congress to cancel it, as current law allows.
yes: The 1974 law's 45-day process

refuse_to_spend.t: A president can refuse to spend money on programs the president considers wasteful.
yes: Presidents withholding approved money, for any president
no: Requiring presidents to spend as directed

refuse_to_spend_cases: The president must spend money Congress approved for this: {case}.
The president can refuse to spend money Congress approved for this: {case}.

emergency_duration.t: No special emergency powers until Congress votes to approve.
yes: Requiring a vote of Congress before emergency powers start

emergency_duration.t: Emergencies should last 30 days, then need Congress's approval.
yes: A 30-day limit without a vote

emergency_duration.t: Emergencies should last 6 months, then need Congress's approval.
yes: A 6-month limit without a vote

emergency_duration.t: Emergencies should last as long as the president decides, as today.
yes: Today's open-ended emergency powers

emergency_funding.t: A president should never use an emergency to spend money Congress refused.
yes: Keeping spending decisions with Congress
no: Emergency declarations to fund rejected projects

emergency_funding.t: Only for a sudden threat, like an attack, until Congress can act.
yes: Short-term emergency spending after an attack
no: Using emergencies for projects Congress rejected

emergency_funding.t: A president can declare an emergency to fund projects whenever the need seems urgent.
yes: Emergency spending on projects Congress refused, by any president

emergency_funding_cases: A president should not be able to use an emergency to pay for this after Congress refused: {case}.
A president should be able to use an emergency to pay for this after Congress refused: {case}.

civil_service.t: Career government employees should be protected from firing over policy disagreements.
yes: Civil service protections for scientists and analysts
no: Firing staff for disagreeing with the president

civil_service.t: Only senior employees who help make policy should be fireable over disagreements.
yes: Fewer protections for senior policy staff

civil_service.t: Most federal employees should be fireable at will.
yes: Ending most civil service protections

independent_agencies.t: Keep independent agencies and make more agencies independent.
yes: Protecting agency leaders from firing over policy
Adding more independent agencies
no: Presidents firing agency heads at will

independent_agencies.t: Keep the independent agencies we have.
yes: Today's protections for the Fed, FTC and similar agencies

independent_agencies.t: Keep only the Federal Reserve independent.
yes: Letting the president fire leaders of the FTC, SEC and others

independent_agencies.t: The president should be able to fire any agency leader.
yes: Ending independence for all agencies, including the Fed

prosecute_opponents.t: A president should never be involved in deciding whom the Justice Department investigates.
yes: Leaving investigations to career prosecutors

prosecute_opponents.t: A president can raise concerns, but career prosecutors decide.
yes: Presidents flagging concerns without ordering investigations

prosecute_opponents.t: A president can order investigations of specific people the president believes broke the law.
yes: Presidents directing investigations, including of opponents, for any president
no: Keeping presidents out of these decisions

pardon_allies.t: Presidents should never pardon family, associates or allies; amend the Constitution to forbid it.
yes: A constitutional ban on self-serving pardons

pardon_allies.t: Pardoning family or allies is legal, but presidents should almost never do it.
yes: Keeping the power while strongly discouraging its use

pardon_allies.t: It's acceptable for a president to pardon family or allies treated unfairly.
yes: Pardons of allies the president believes were treated unfairly

accept_results.t: A candidate who lost should concede once courts and officials confirm the result.
yes: Conceding after results are confirmed

accept_results.t: A candidate can accept the result but keep saying publicly it was stolen.
yes: Accepting the outcome while disputing it in public

accept_results.t: A candidate should keep fighting, including asking legislators to overturn the result.
yes: Pressing legislators to overturn confirmed results

accept_results.t: A candidate should refuse to accept the result and urge supporters to resist.
yes: Refusing to concede and calling on supporters to resist

s.t: No single leader should be able to act without others agreeing, even if needed changes take years.
yes: Requiring Congress, courts and the Senate to sign off on major moves
no: Presidents acting alone to speed things up

s.t: On balance, no single leader should be able to act without others agreeing, even if needed changes take years.
yes: Requiring Congress, courts and the Senate to sign off on major moves
no: Presidents acting alone to speed things up

s.t: On balance, an elected leader should be able to act quickly, even with fewer checks on mistakes or abuse.
yes: Presidents acting without waiting for Congress or courts
no: Checks that delay what voters chose

s.t: An elected leader should be able to act quickly, even with fewer checks on mistakes or abuse.
yes: Presidents acting without waiting for Congress or courts
no: Checks that delay what voters chose

torn.t: You weigh checks and quick action about equally.
means: You'd let leaders act fast in a crisis but keep checks in normal times

s.t: Courts should strike down unconstitutional laws even when most voters support them.
yes: Courts overturning popular laws that violate rights
no: Courts deferring to majorities on rights

s.t: On balance, courts should strike down unconstitutional laws even when most voters support them.
yes: Courts overturning popular laws that violate rights
no: Courts deferring to majorities on rights

s.t: On balance, courts should rarely overrule laws most voters clearly support, even if some people's rights are limited.
yes: Letting popular laws stand
Narrower court review
no: Courts overturning laws with majority support

s.t: Courts should rarely overrule laws most voters clearly support, even if some people's rights are limited.
yes: Letting popular laws stand
Narrower court review
no: Courts overturning laws with majority support

torn.t: You weigh court review and majority rule about equally.
means: You'd want courts to step in only when rights are clearly violated

filibuster.t: Expand the 60-vote rule to nominations for judges and cabinet posts.
yes: Requiring 60 votes to confirm judges and cabinet members

filibuster.t: Keep the 60-vote rule as it is.
yes: Today's filibuster

filibuster.t: Keep the 60-vote rule, but make senators who block a bill stay and speak on the floor.
yes: A talking filibuster

filibuster.t: End the 60-vote rule for some bills, like voting rights or budget bills.
yes: Majority votes for selected kinds of bills

filibuster.t: End the 60-vote rule; a simple majority should pass bills.
yes: Abolishing the filibuster, whichever party is in charge

filibuster_cases: This should still need 60 votes in the Senate: {case}.
A simple majority of 51 senators should be able to pass this: {case}.

rule_bending_leader.t: It's never acceptable for a president to bend or work around laws, court rulings or official procedures.
yes: Presidents following laws and rulings even when they block their agenda
no: Working around rules to deliver for voters

rule_bending_leader.t: Bending the rules is acceptable only in a real emergency.
yes: Bending rules in true emergencies
no: Bending rules to get policies through

rule_bending_leader.t: Bending the rules is acceptable when they clearly stand in the way of what voters chose.
yes: Working around laws or rulings that block an elected agenda

rule_bending_leader.t: The country needs a leader willing to bend the rules.
yes: A president who works around laws, rulings and procedures

political_violence.t: Political violence is never justified in the US today.
means: No cause justifies violence, whoever is in power

political_violence.t: Violence is justified only against a government that has seized power illegally.
means: Violence is acceptable only if the constitutional order has been overthrown

political_violence.t: Violence is sometimes justified when peaceful methods have failed.
means: After peaceful efforts fail, violence for a political cause can be acceptable

court_expansion.t: Congress should add justices when the party in power wants different rulings.
yes: Adding justices to change the Court's majority, for either party

court_expansion.t: Change the Court's size only as part of a bipartisan reform.
yes: Bipartisan changes to the Court
no: One party adding justices on its own

court_expansion.t: Keep the Supreme Court at 9 justices.
yes: Keeping 9 justices

presidential_immunity.t: Former presidents can be prosecuted like anyone else.
yes: Overturning broad presidential immunity

presidential_immunity.t: Former presidents are immune only for core constitutional duties.
yes: Immunity for duties like pardons and commanding the military only

presidential_immunity.t: Former presidents are immune for all official acts.
yes: The 2024 ruling's broad immunity
no: Prosecuting former presidents for official acts

press_retaliation.t: A president should never punish news outlets for their coverage.
yes: Protecting outlets' licenses and press access regardless of coverage
no: Pulling access or licenses over coverage

press_retaliation.t: A president can limit outlets' access to events like briefings, not licenses.
yes: Restricting access to briefings

press_retaliation.t: A president can punish outlets the president believes spread falsehoods.
yes: Pulling licenses or access from outlets, for any president

agency_deference.t: Courts should usually defer to agency experts when a law is unclear.
yes: Restoring deference to agencies

agency_deference.t: Courts should defer to agencies only on technical or scientific questions.
yes: Deference on scientific and technical matters

agency_deference.t: Judges should decide what unclear laws mean themselves.
yes: The 2024 ruling ending deference

president_court_ruling.t: A president should comply fully with a court ruling while appealing, and avoid attacking the judge.
yes: Complying and appealing quietly

president_court_ruling.t: A president should comply while appealing, but can criticize the judge publicly.
yes: Complying while criticizing the judge

president_court_ruling.t: A president should comply only if a higher court agrees.
yes: Waiting for appeals before complying

president_court_ruling.t: A president can ignore a ruling the president believes is wrong.
yes: Presidents disregarding court rulings, for any president
